findings.title: Hardcoded GitHub Personal Access Token in C header
findings.description: A GitHub PAT is embedded as a preprocessor macro in a shipped header. Anyone with the source (or the compiled binary's string table) can extract the token and gain whatever repository access the token's scopes grant, including pushing code or exfiltrating private repos. Rotation is required, and secrets must come from the environment or a secret manager at runtime.

ai_assessments.rationale:
I've verified everything I can. Here is my assessment.

## What the evidence shows

`src/vuln_secret.h` is a 4-line header whose only content is a secret constant:

```c
#ifndef CONFIG_H
#define CONFIG_H
#define GITHUB_PAT "[REDACTED]"
#endif
```

Confirmed directly by reading the file, and corroborated by a second independent finding on the same line (`model-0cd0f4bb77912512`). A grep across the snapshot for `GITHUB_PAT` / `vuln_secret` returns exactly one hit: the definition itself. `src/safe_header.h` is the contrasting clean case, where the macro holds only the PEM header prefix (`-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----\n`) and no key material.

The CWE-798 classification is correct: a credential is committed to source as a compile-time constant, so it is exposed to every repo reader, clone, fork, and git history, and it is baked into any binary built from the header. Rotation requires a rebuild.

## What I could not verify

These gaps matter for how confidently the *impact* can be stated:

- **Token content and validity.** The value is redacted by the tooling in every output, including the raw observation snippet. I cannot confirm it is a live, well-formed GitHub PAT, nor determine its scopes. A `ghp_`-prefixed token with `repo` and `workflow` scope is a serious supply-chain risk; a revoked or dummy placeholder is a hygiene defect only.
- **Reachability.** No code in the snapshot includes `vuln_secret.h` or references `GITHUB_PAT`, and no build file, Makefile, or CMakeLists is present. The scanner's "shipped header" and "compiled binary's string table" claims are assertions about how the project builds, not something I can observe here. If the header is never included, the "in binary" path is unproven, though the source-exposure path stands regardless.
- **Scanner coverage.** Gitleaks and Semgrep are both absent from PATH on this host, so my independent secret-detection check returned `skipped`/`failed` rather than clean. `check_coverage` for CWE-798 returned no records. T

The hardened sibling image uses a distroless nonroot base with an explicit UID.

ai_assessments.rationale:
## Assessment: model-193a6e1b4a7207d0

**Confirmed, with one correction to the scanner's framing.**

`docker/vuln/Dockerfile` (4 lines, read in full):
```
FROM ubuntu:latest
USER root
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
CMD ["/bin/bash"]
```

The scanner's headline is slightly off. It says "the image never switches to an unprivileged user," implying an omission. In fact line 2 is an *explicit* `USER root` directive. That matters because a remediation that merely adds `USER` somewhere, or assumes the base image defaults, misses that root is deliberately declared here and must be actively overridden.

**The impact is worse than the finding states.** The scanner reasoned about container-internal root and hypothetical escape. The actual deployment raises this to host-level. `deploy/vuln_pod.yaml` runs `ubuntu:latest` with `privileged: true` and `runAsUser: 0`. A privileged container with a root shell as its default `CMD` and root-owned mounts is not a container-escape *risk*; it is a container-escape *configuration*. The `docker/safe` and `deploy/safe` pair show the intended contrast: distroless nonroot base, `USER 65532:65532`, `runAsNonRoot`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, `capabilities.drop: ALL`, `automountServiceAccountToken: [REDACTED]

**Two factors that bound severity.** There is no application code in this image at all: it is a base image plus `curl`, with `/bin/bash` as the entrypoint. There is no in-repo attack surface to exploit for initial code execution, so the root user is a *multiplier* on an external compromise rather than a directly reachable flaw. I also cannot see from source whether this manifest is deployed to production, what host paths are mounted, or whether the cluster enforces Pod Security Standards that would reject `privileged`. All of that is unknown, not safe.

**Coverage is genuinely weak.** Every deterministic tool was unavailable: Trivy not on PATH, Semgrep not on PATH, and the coverage record shows

ai_assessments.rationale: Confirmed by direct read of deploy/vuln_pod.yaml (11 lines, read in full): the Pod spec at line 5 has no automountServiceAccountToken field and no serviceAccountName, so Kubernetes' default (true) applies and the 'default' ServiceAccount token is projected into the container at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. The defect is real and the remediation is a one-line change. Severity is argued lower than the reported medium: this is defense-in-depth layered on the already-critical privileged/root configuration, since a privileged container can read node and other-pod credentials via container escape regardless of this pod's automount setting. I confirmed the finding against the actual manifest. Note that `inspect_code` returned line 11 as the last line with `runAsUser: 0`, and the raw snippet agrees; there is no `runAsNonRoot`, no `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, no capability drop, and no `automountServiceAccountToken: [REDACTED] anywhere in the file.

## Assessment

**What the code shows (confirmed, read this turn)**

`deploy/vuln_pod.yaml` is an 11-line Pod manifest:

- Line 8: `image: ubuntu:latest` -- mutable tag, non-pinned.
- Line 10: `privileged: true` -- full device and kernel-capability access.
- Line 11: `runAsUser: 0` -- explicitly forces UID 0.
- No `runAsNonRoot`, no `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, no `capabilities.drop`, no `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, no `automountServiceAccountToken: [REDACTED]

The sibling `deploy/safe_pod.yaml` is a hardened control: `runAsNonRoot: true`, `runAsUser: 65532`, distroless nonroot image, read-only rootfs, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, `drop: ["ALL"]`. So the vulnerable manifest is deliberately insecure by contrast, and the correct remediation shape already exists in the repo.

**Is the finding accurate?** Yes, on the narrow claim. `runAsUser: 0` sets UID 0, and the absence of `runAsNonRoot: true` means the kubelet performs no rejection check against a root-capable image. That is a genuine misconfiguration and the observation's stated remedy is correct.

**Two corrections to the finding's framing, both of which matter for severity**

1. **`privileged: true` is the dominant defect, not the UID.** A privileged container gets all Linux capabilities and full host device access. Even with `runAsUser: 65532` and `runAsNonRoot: true`, a privileged container can trivially regain effective root inside the container and has far greater reach than UID 0 alone. So this finding is a true but *secondary* weakness sitting on top of a worse one. If the UID issue alone were fixed, the pod would still be critically exposed. The missing control is a digest-pinned, minimal image.

## Assessment: model-b5e12cfc2239861f

**Evidence confirmed.** `deploy/vuln_pod.yaml` line 8 reads exactly `image: ubuntu:latest`, with no `@sha256:` digest. The container also sets `privileged: true` and `runAsUser: 0`. The sibling `deploy/safe_pod.yaml` pins a distroless tag and hardens the context, so the two files form a deliberate insecure/hardened pair.

**What the finding actually covers.** The core claim -- a mutable tag with no digest pin, so the executed image is whatever the registry resolves at pull time -- is factually correct and verifiable in the file. Two parts of the narrative need separating out:

- *Supply-chain risk (this finding's subject)*: tag retargeting, registry or mirror poisoning, or an unreviewed upstream republish lands code in the workload. This is real but **conditional** on attacker control of the `library/ubuntu` tag or a registry path. That is a meaningful precondition, not a trivially reachable one.
- *Amplification*: the scanner says compromise here yields execution "inside a privileged, root-running container." True, and confirmed by lines 9-11. But that severity belongs to the privileged/root findings (`model-8d2763e75b3679a9`, `model-da52a917cd61585d`, `model-8c8acb05feb5dc1e`), which are already tracked as critical/high. Counting the container-escape impact twice here would inflate this medium into something it isn't. I'm scoring the pinning defect on its own.

The closest fit would be CWE-1357 (Reliance on Insufficiently Trustworthy Component) or CWE-829, but I'm not asserting a reclassification without rule metadata.

## Assessment: `model-5325207d51d0ee12`

**The finding is confirmed at the code level, but it is a build hygiene issue, not an exploitable vulnerability.** The scanner's own description mixes two claims (non-reproducibility and tag poisoning) and one factual overreach, which I'll separate below.

### Evidence verified

`docker/vuln/Dockerfile` is 4 lines, read in full:

```
1: FROM ubuntu:latest
2: USER root
3: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
4: CMD ["/bin/bash"]
```

Every element of the observation is present: floating `latest` tag, no digest, no `curl` version pin, no `--no-install-recommends`, and no `rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*`. The sibling `docker/safe/Dockerfile` is the hardened contrast case (`gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot`, `USER 65532:65532`, `ENTRYPOINT`), which corroborates that this file is a deliberately insecure fixture.

`deploy/vuln_pod.yaml:8` also uses `image: ubuntu:latest`, so the floating tag propagates to the deploy manifest. That is a separate finding's territory, not this one's, but it means the pattern is not confined to one file.

### Where the observation overreaches

"**a tag-poisoning attacker controls the base layer of a root-running image**" overstates this finding. Tag poisoning requires a compromise of the upstream registry or the maintainer account, an upstream precondition with no evidence in this repo. The finding as scoped (line 1 plus the unpinned `curl` install) describes reproducibility loss and an unreviewed upstream change surface. The "root-running" half of that sentence belongs to `model-193a6e1b4a7207d0` and `model-158337abf744790d`, which correctly own the `USER root` issue. Severity is being inflated by borrowing impact from a sibling finding.

**Verdict: confirmed (as a supply-chain hygiene defect, not a directly exploitable vulnerability).**

What I read in this turn:
- `docker/vuln/Dockerfile` (4 lines total, read in full via `inspect_code`): line 1 is exactly `FROM ubuntu:latest`. No digest, no explicit version.
- `grep_code` over `*Dockerfile*` for `^FROM`: two Dockerfiles in the snapshot. `docker/safe/Dockerfile:1` is `FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot` (tag-pinned, nonroot); `docker/vuln/Dockerfile:1` is the flagged `ubuntu:latest`. No other Dockerfile uses a floating tag in this pattern search.
- `query_scanner_findings` on `docker/vuln`: seven findings on this same 4-line file, including a duplicate of this exact issue (`model-ec789c1ecd33430d`, severity low) and a root-user finding (`model-193a6e1b4a7207d0`, high). This is a deliberately paired vuln/safe fixture, which supports "real defect in a test fixture" rather than production risk.
- `run_config_audit` (iac_config) on `docker/vuln`: **skipped**, Trivy is not on PATH. So no independent IaC scanner corroboration exists; the finding rests on direct source reading plus the native-hunt observation.

Why it holds: `ubuntu:latest` is a moving reference. The image pulled at build time is not the image that was reviewed, builds are not byte-reproducible, and a retagged or compromised upstream tag enters the build silently. The sibling `docker/safe/Dockerfile` shows the project already knows the pinned-digest pattern, so the delta is a real deviation, not an unavoidable constraint.

There is no attacker-controlled input in the Dockerfile itself, and the practical impact is conditional on an upstream tag compromise or an unnoticed regressed base. findings.title: Hardcoded credential committed in source header
findings.description: The snapshot contains a dedicated header whose entire purpose is to embed a secret constant in source. Any secret written into a repository is exposed to everyone with read access to the repo, to every clone and fork, and to anything built from it; it cannot be rotated without a rebuild and it survives in git history after deletion. This is the single highest-impact item in the snapshot: a committed credential is directly usable by anyone who reads the file. No scanner confirmed this (trivy config audit was skipped, and no secret scan returned results in this turn), so the finding rests on code inspection only. The exact literal is deliberately not reproduced here; the file and line are the actionable evidence.

findings.title: Container image runs as root
findings.description: The insecure Dockerfile in the docker/vuln vs docker/safe pair does not drop to a non-root user, so the process runs as UID 0 inside the container. Any code-execution bug in the application then has root inside the container, which raises the impact of a container escape and lets the process modify its own image filesystem and any writable mount. The safe Dockerfile is the contrast case and is not reported. Severity is medium because root-in-container alone is not an escape; it matters in combination with the pod issues above.

findings.title: Unpinned mutable base image tag in build
findings.description: Building from a floating or 'latest'-style tag means the image content changes without any commit in this repository, so builds are not reproducible and a compromised or regressed upstream tag is pulled silently on the next build. Pinning by digest is the fix. Low severity: it is a supply-chain hygiene issue rather than a directly exploitable bug, and it is listed separately from the root-user finding because it is a different defect at a different fix.
